The question of whether clams have eyes is genuinely contested across the retrieved sources. Multiple scientific and peer-reviewed sources confirm that various clam species do possess eyes: d1 (NCBI) describes pit eyes in some bivalves, compound eyes in ark clams, and pinhole eyes in giant clams, while d4 (BioMed Central) confirms ark clams can have 200–300 compound eyes along the mantle edge. d7 (Wikipedia) states that giant clams (Tridacna) have ocelli that allow light to penetrate their mantles, and d10 (EvoDevo journal) notes that while most adult bivalves lack eyes, ark clams possess sophisticated compound eyes. d2 and d3 add that giant clams possess several hundred small pinhole eyes (hyaline organs) on the exposed mantle that detect changes in light levels. However, directly contradicting these findings, d12 (Florida Fish and Wildlife Commission, an official government source) states "Clams have no eyes, but they respond to touch, vibrations and chemical cues," and d11 similarly asserts "Clams have no eyes, ears, or noses, so they cannot see, hear, or smell," with d8 echoing the same claim. The most likely resolution, supported by the weight of scientific evidence in d1, d4, d7, and d10, is that the answer depends on the species: many clam species (especially giant clams and ark clams) do possess light-sensitive eyes or ocelli, while the blanket claim that "clams have no eyes" appears to be an oversimplification found in less specialized sources [d12, d11, d8].
